intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit seven: international organizations, part one.

slides.3: Two roots: administrative unions and peace organizations. International organizations grew from two different impulses. Administrative unions were technical organizations solving cross-border coordination problems — the International Telegraph Union of 1865 and the Universal Postal Union of 1874. Peace organizations were political, starting with the League of Nations in 1919. That distinction between technical and political organizations survives today as one of the axes along which they are classified.
slides.4: The characteristics of an international organization — five features gathered around the concept. A founding treaty governed by international law, which functions as the organization's constitution. Members: states, and also other organizations. Organs that decide for the organization, and adopt and implement its decisions. Establishment for the long term, described as institutionalized cooperation. And a seat, regulated by a headquarters agreement. Running through all five is a permanent tension between integration and sovereignty: every competence the organization gains, a member has given up.
slides.7: The personality of an international organization is derivative and functional. Two contrasts carry this. A state's international legal personality is original; an organization's is derivative — it extends only as far as the members transferred it. And it is functional: not only the powers written into the founding treaty, but also those necessary for the organization to fulfil its tasks effectively. That is the implied powers doctrine, established in the Bernadotte opinion of 1949. The flip side is ultra vires: an organization acting beyond its competences acts without legal basis.
slides.17: The other three kinds of organ. Beyond the representative and administrative pair there are three more: parliamentary bodies, as in the European Union and the Council of Europe; expert bodies, such as the International Law Commission; and judicial bodies — the International Court of Justice and the United Nations Administrative Tribunal, or the Court of Justice of the European Union. Note where the International Law Commission sits: it is an expert organ of the United Nations, which is why its draft articles are authoritative without being binding.
slides.21: Why organizations have immunity — and how far it goes. States grant immunity by treaty, in the founding treaty or the headquarters agreement, and the purpose is stated plainly: interference by state authorities or courts must not affect the organization's functioning. That makes it functional immunity in principle. But here is the practical truth, and it is the exam point: in practice it operates as absolute immunity before domestic courts, with no distinction between private and sovereign acts — unlike state immunity, where exactly that distinction decides.
slides.22: What the immunity package contains — three further elements. Alternative dispute settlement: arbitral or administrative tribunals, especially for employment disputes, which is the price of shutting claimants out of domestic courts. Buildings, archives and other assets are inviolable — and inviolable is not the same as extraterritorial: the territory remains the host state's, the authorities simply may not enter. And extensive tax exemptions.
slides.23: The Vienna International Centre: the United Nations complex on the Donaustadt side of Vienna, the Y-shaped towers with the Danube behind. It is the physical object that the headquarters agreement, coming next, is about.
slides.25: Inviolability in the actual text. Article three, section fifteen does three things at once, and together they show how carefully inviolability is drafted. Austria recognises the inviolability of the seat, which is under United Nations control and authority. But, second, Austrian law applies within the seat, except as otherwise provided. And third, Austrian courts have jurisdiction over acts done and transactions taking place within the seat. Section sixteen then lets the United Nations make regulations operative within the seat, and provides that inconsistent Austrian law is inapplicable to the extent of the inconsistency — with fire protection and sanitary regulations expressly preserved. This is the concrete proof of the point just made: inviolable, but not extraterritorial.
